title: Sharding and Partitioning
summary: Choose range, hash or directory partitioning, defend a partition key, handle hot keys and cross-shard queries, and reshard online.
body:
A single database node eventually runs out of something: disk for the data set, write throughput on the primary, memory for the working set, or simply blast radius when it fails. Partitioning splits the data so that each piece is small enough to manage; sharding places those pieces on different machines. In an interview, sharding is a deep-dive topic you should reach only after an estimate shows that one node (plus replicas) is not enough. When you do, the interviewer expects a defended partition key, a plan for hot keys, an honest account of cross-shard queries, and a way to add capacity without downtime.

## Vertical versus horizontal partitioning

**Vertical partitioning** splits by columns or by function. Rarely-read large columns (a user's profile photo blob, a long biography) move to a separate table or store; or whole domains (billing, catalogue, messaging) move to separate databases owned by separate services. It is cheap and often the first step, but each domain is still bounded by one node.

**Horizontal partitioning** splits rows: users 1–10 million on one partition, the next 10 million on another. When those partitions live on different nodes, it is called sharding. Each shard has the same schema and usually its own replicas. Some databases (Cassandra, DynamoDB, CockroachDB, Vitess for MySQL) shard automatically; with plain PostgreSQL or MySQL the application or a proxy must route queries.

## Partitioning schemes

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    App["App servers"] --> R["Shard router"]
    R --> M[("Shard map: key range or hash range to shard")]
    R --> S1[("Shard 1 + replicas")]
    R --> S2[("Shard 2 + replicas")]
    R --> S3[("Shard 3 + replicas")]
```

The router computes which shard owns a key using a shard map, then sends the query there. The map may be a formula (hash modulo), a sorted list of ranges, or an explicit lookup table; it can live in a client library, a proxy tier, or a coordination service.

| Scheme | How a key is placed | Strength | Weakness |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Range | Contiguous key ranges per shard | Efficient range scans; easy to split a hot range | Monotonic keys (timestamps, sequential IDs) send all writes to the last range |
| Hash | Hash of key decides shard | Even spread of keys and writes | Range queries hit every shard; naive modulo remaps most keys when the count changes |
| Directory | Lookup table maps each key or tenant to a shard | Can move individual tenants; supports uneven placement | Extra lookup on every request; the directory must be highly available and cached |

Many systems combine them: hash the key into a fixed number of logical partitions, then assign ranges of logical partitions to physical nodes with a small directory.

## Choosing a partition key

A good partition key has three properties:

1. **High cardinality.** Millions of distinct values, so data can spread across many shards. Country code is a poor key; user ID is a good one.
2. **Even access.** Traffic, not just data, spreads evenly. A key whose few values receive most requests creates a hot shard.
3. **Query alignment.** The most frequent queries include the key, so they touch one shard. For a chat app, partitioning messages by `conversation_id` makes "load this conversation" a single-shard read; partitioning by `message_id` would scatter it.

Write the top three queries next to your candidate key and check each one. If a frequent query cannot supply the key, you need a secondary index or a second copy of the data keyed differently.

## Hot partitions

Even a good key can produce a hot partition: a celebrity's posts, a viral product, a single giant tenant. Mitigations, from simplest to most invasive:

- **Cache** hot reads in front of the shard. This handles most read hot spots.
- **Replicate reads** for the hot partition across more replicas.
- **Salt the key**: write to `item_id#0` … `item_id#9` chosen randomly, spreading writes over ten partitions; reads must gather all ten and combine them. Good for counters and append-heavy keys.
- **Split** the hot range (range sharding) or move a large tenant to a dedicated shard (directory sharding).
- **Change the access pattern**: buffer and batch writes for a hot counter instead of updating one row per event.

Detect hot spots with per-partition request and byte metrics; an average across shards hides them.

## Cross-shard queries and transactions

Queries that do not include the partition key become scatter-gather: the router sends them to every shard and merges results. Latency is set by the slowest shard, and load multiplies with shard count, so keep these off the hot path or serve them from a separate index.

Transactions spanning shards need coordination. Two-phase commit gives atomicity but holds locks across a network round trip and blocks if the coordinator fails mid-protocol. A saga breaks the operation into local transactions with compensating actions, accepting temporary inconsistency. The best option is usually to avoid the need: co-locate data that changes together under the same partition key (a user's cart and its items), and design invariants to be checkable within one shard.

## Resharding without downtime

Adding shards means moving data while serving traffic. With hash modulo N, changing N moves most keys, which is why systems instead use consistent hashing with virtual nodes, or a fixed large number of logical partitions (say 1,024) that are reassigned between nodes as whole units. Either way, only the moved partitions migrate.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as App
    participant Old as Old shard
    participant New as New shard
    Note over App,New: Phase 1 dual write
    App->>Old: Write
    App->>New: Write (same key)
    Note over Old,New: Phase 2 backfill historical rows
    Old->>New: Copy rows in batches
    Note over App,New: Phase 3 verify, then switch reads
    App->>New: Read
    Note over App,Old: Phase 4 stop writes to old, clean up
```

The migration first writes new changes to both locations, then backfills existing rows, compares counts or checksums, flips reads to the new shard, and finally stops writing to the old one. Backfill must not overwrite newer dual-written rows, so use version numbers or "insert if absent" semantics. Managed systems perform a similar copy-then-cut-over internally when they split partitions.

## Secondary indexes on sharded data

| Index type | Where index entries live | Writes | Reads by indexed field |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Local (document-partitioned) | Same shard as the row | Single-shard, transactional with the row | Scatter-gather across all shards |
| Global (term-partitioned) | Partitioned by the indexed value | Touch the row's shard and the index's shard; often updated asynchronously | Single index partition, then fetch rows |

DynamoDB's global secondary indexes, for example, are updated asynchronously and support only eventually consistent reads. Choose local indexes when queries usually include the partition key anyway; choose global indexes when a frequent query does not, and accept index lag.

## Failure modes and interview mistakes

- Sharding before showing that one primary with replicas and caching cannot cope.
- Choosing a partition key that the main query cannot supply.
- Range-partitioning by creation time and sending every insert to one shard.
- Ignoring the cost of re-routing when a shard fails or moves; clients must refresh their shard map.
- Promising cross-shard transactions without naming the protocol or its failure behavior.

## How to use it in an interview

Justify sharding with numbers: "Five years is 36 TB before replication, so I will partition by user_id using hashed logical partitions." Then walk through the top queries, hot-key handling, and how you will add shards. Expect follow-ups such as "a celebrity has 50 million followers," "how do you query by email?" and "what happens during a rebalance?"

## Interview exercise

An e-commerce order service must support "orders for a customer, newest first" and "all orders for a seller in the past day." Pick a partition key, explain which query becomes scatter-gather or needs a global index, and describe what you do when one seller generates 30% of all orders.

## Further reading

- [Vitess documentation: Sharding](https://vitess.io/docs/reference/features/sharding/) explains keyspace IDs, vindexes and resharding for MySQL.
- [Amazon DynamoDB: Best practices for designing partition keys](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/bp-partition-key-design.html) covers key cardinality and write sharding.
- [Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store](https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf) describes consistent hashing with virtual nodes.
keyTakeaways: Shard only after an estimate shows one primary with replicas and caching cannot meet storage or write demand.
A partition key needs high cardinality, even access, and alignment with the most frequent queries.
Hot partitions need targeted fixes: caching, key salting, splitting or isolating a large tenant.
Avoid cross-shard transactions by co-locating data that changes together; otherwise name 2PC or a saga and its failure behavior.
Reshard by moving whole logical partitions with dual writes, backfill, verification and a read cut-over.
Local secondary indexes keep writes single-shard but scatter reads; global indexes do the reverse and often lag.
